topic: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
parentTitle: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
title: Transition to adult services
blurb: Plan a young person's move from children's to adult services early, with a named worker, the young person at the centre and the legal milestones in place.
question: Jasmine is 13 and in year 8. She has a severe learning disability, epilepsy and an education, health and care (EHC) plan. Her mother is worried about 'falling off a cliff' at 18. When should planning start, who should coordinate it, and what will continue after 18?

teach.body: Moving from children's to adults' services means new teams, new rules, different thresholds and, often, losing professionals the family has known for years. For young people with a learning disability and complex health needs, gaps in care at this point can be dangerous. NICE NG43 sets out how to make the move gradual, person-centred and coordinated. In plain English: start early, plan with the young person, give them one named person, and do not let support stop on a birthday.

items.label: Planning for adulthood starts at the latest
Annual health checks on GP LD register
Adult services, at a time of stability

teach.caption: Young people leaving care: planning must start from age 15 and a half.

teach.body: Start planning for adulthood from year 9 (age 13 or 14) at the latest, or immediately if the young person enters services close to transfer (1.2.1). For those with EHC plans, the annual review from year 9 must consider preparation for adulthood (SEND Regulations 2014 reg 20(6)). The point of transfer should not be based on a rigid age threshold and should take place at a time of relative stability (1.2.3). Hold an annual transition review with the young person, family and all practitioners, including the GP (1.2.4).

items.label: minimum support before AND after transfer (1.2.9)
adult appointments with the same practitioner (1.4.4)

teach.caption: The named worker could be a nurse, youth worker, GP, AHP or existing keyworker with a meaningful relationship with the young person.

head: Law
What it gives
Section
rows: EHC plan to end of academic year at 25
Child's needs assessment if likely adult needs
teach.caption: Care Act s58: the local authority must assess where a child is likely to have needs after 18 and assessment would be of significant benefit, with the consent condition met.

teach.h: The young person at the centre
teach.body: NG43 asks for person-centred, strengths-based support that treats the young person as an equal partner, agrees goals with them and builds their confidence to direct their own care. Plans cover education and employment, community inclusion, health and wellbeing, and independent living and housing. Use communication passports or one-page profiles, and consider a personal folder shared with adult services, including preferences about parent involvement.

Planning for Jasmine must start in year 9, next year, through her EHC plan reviews. Her community learning disability nurse, whom Jasmine knows well, becomes her named worker. Each year a review involves Jasmine (with symbols and her communication passport), her mother, school, the paediatric epilepsy team and the GP. Before 18 the local authority completes a Care Act child's needs assessment. Her EHC plan can continue to 25 while she is in education. Adult epilepsy and LD teams meet her before transfer, and the named worker stays involved for at least six months afterwards.

teach.text: At 16 the Mental Capacity Act applies and at 18 parents no longer make decisions for their adult child. Presume the young person has capacity, give all practicable support to decide, and if they lack capacity for a specific decision, decide in their best interests while consulting family. Parents remain important, but their role changes.

teach.h: If the young person disengages after transfer

steps.label: Review the plan
steps.sub: Find another way to meet needs

teach.caption: NG43 1.4.1-1.4.3: work within safeguarding protocols; do not simply discharge.

items: Start planning from year 9 (13-14) at the latest; immediately if late to services.
A named worker coordinates and supports at least 6 months before and after transfer.
Transfer at a time of relative stability, not on a rigid birthday.
EHC plans can continue to 25; Care Act s58 assessment before 18.
MCA from 16: the young person is the decision-maker unless they lack capacity for that decision.

summary: You can now plan transition to adult services in line with NICE NG43: starting by year 9, with a named worker, annual reviews and transfer at a stable time. You can explain EHC plans to 25, the Care Act child's needs assessment and how the MCA changes decision-making from 16.

A.q: Jasmine is 13 and in year 8. She has a severe learning disability and an EHC plan. Her mother asks when planning for adulthood must start. What is the correct answer?
options: From year 11, when she is 15 or 16
From year 9, at age 13 or 14
From age 17, a year before transfer
From age 16, when the MCA applies
A.why: NICE NG43 1.2.1: start planning from year 9 (age 13 or 14) at the latest; for young people with EHC plans this must happen from year 9 under the SEND Regulations 2014 reg 20(6), made under the Children and Families Act 2014.

whyNot.0: Year 11 is later than the year 9 requirement.
whyNot.2: A year before transfer is far too late.
whyNot.3: MCA age is a separate milestone; planning starts earlier.

A.q: Kai, 16, has a learning disability and complex health needs. Many professionals are involved in his transition, and his family find it confusing. What does NICE NG43 recommend?
options: A monthly multi-agency meeting chaired by the GP
Separate transition plans for health and social care
A named worker to coordinate his transition
A single meeting at 18 to hand over to adult teams
A.why: NG43 1.2.5-1.2.7: help the young person identify a single practitioner as named worker to coordinate transition care and support and link with other practitioners.

whyNot.0: NG43 sets an annual review, not monthly meetings, and coordination sits with a named worker.
whyNot.1: Separate plans increase fragmentation; NG43 asks for integrated working.
whyNot.3: A single handover meeting at 18 is the 'cliff edge' NG43 aims to avoid.

A.q: A learning disability nurse is the named worker for Ollie, 17, who is moving to adult services. For how long should she support him?
options: A minimum of 6 months before and after transfer
Until his 18th birthday, then hand over the role
For 3 months before transfer and no time after
For one year after transfer to adult services
A.why: NG43 1.2.9: support for the time defined in legislation or a minimum of 6 months before and after transfer, negotiated with the young person.

whyNot.1: Stopping at 18 creates a gap at the point of transfer.
whyNot.2: Support must continue after transfer too.
whyNot.3: NICE sets 6 months before and after as a minimum, not one year after only.

B.q: Tara, 17, has a profound learning disability. Her family worry her care package will stop at 18. Which assessment should the local authority carry out before she turns 18?
options: A child's needs assessment under the Care Act
A carer's assessment for her parents
A continuing healthcare checklist on her 18th birthday
A deprivation of liberty assessment
B.why: Care Act 2014 s58: where a child is likely to have needs for care and support after 18, the local authority must assess if it would be of significant benefit and the consent condition is met.

whyNot.1: Her parents may need a carer's assessment too, but it does not assess Tara's own needs.
whyNot.2: Continuing healthcare is a separate NHS process and does not replace the Care Act assessment.
whyNot.3: DoLS assessment concerns liberty, not her care and support needs after 18.

B.q: Marcus, 19, has a learning disability and an EHC plan and is at a further education college. His mother has been told the plan ends now that he is an adult. What is accurate?
options: It ends at 19 when he leaves school-age education
It ends at 18 and is replaced by an adult care plan
It continues for life while he has a learning disability
It can last until the end of the academic year he is 25
B.why: Children and Families Act 2014 s46: a local authority may maintain an EHC plan until the end of the academic year in which the young person turns 25.

whyNot.0: There is no automatic end at 19.
whyNot.1: EHC plans do not end at 18 and are not replaced by an adult care plan.
whyNot.2: The plan does not continue for life; it can run to age 25.

B.q: Priya, 18, has a learning disability and has just moved to adult services. Her mother is used to making health decisions for her and wants to decide about a new treatment. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept the mother's decision as next of kin
Presume Priya has capacity and support her to decide
Ask the GP to make the decision in Priya's best interests
Wait for a court order before any decision
B.why: MCA 2005 s1(2)-(3): adults (and young people 16+) are presumed to have capacity and must be given all practicable support to decide. Parents remain involved if Priya wishes.

whyNot.0: Next of kin has no legal power to consent for an adult.
whyNot.2: Best interests applies only after a capacity assessment shows she lacks capacity for this decision.
whyNot.3: A court order is not needed for routine treatment decisions.

C.q: Ella, 17, has a learning disability and epilepsy. She is due to move to adult services next month, the same month her family moves house and she starts college. Her seizures have recently increased. What is the best approach?
options: Transfer as planned so adult teams can review her seizures
Transfer now but cancel her college start until next year
Discharge her from children's services and ask the GP to refer
Reconsider timing so transfer happens at a stable point
C.why: NG43 1.2.3: the point of transfer should not be based on a rigid age threshold and should take place at a time of relative stability.

whyNot.0: Several major changes at once, with worsening seizures, make this an unstable time.
whyNot.1: Cancelling college restricts her life to fit a service date.
whyNot.2: Discharge without handover creates a gap in care.

C.q: Sam, 19, has a learning disability and moved to adult services six months ago. He has missed three appointments with the adult LD team. What does NICE NG43 recommend?
options: Discharge him back to his GP after three missed appointments
Contact Sam and his family, follow up and involve the GP
Send a letter saying he must attend or lose the service
Ask children's services to take him back until he is 25
C.why: NG43 1.4.1: if a young person does not attend or engage after transfer, adult services, working within safeguarding protocols, should try to contact the young person and family, follow up and involve other professionals including the GP.

whyNot.0: Discharge without follow-up risks losing him from care.
whyNot.2: A threatening letter is not person-centred and does not explore why he is not attending.
whyNot.3: Children's services do not take back adults; the named worker reviews the plan instead.

C.q: A transition review is being planned for Jordan, 16, who has a moderate learning disability. Which approach best reflects NICE NG43?
options: Professionals agree goals first, then share them with Jordan
His parents attend on his behalf to avoid upsetting him
Jordan is an equal partner and goals are agreed with him
The review focuses on health needs and leaves out housing
C.why: NG43 1.1.4: treat the young person as an equal partner, fully involve them and agree goals with them, covering education, employment, community inclusion, health and independent living.

whyNot.0: Goals are agreed with the young person, not presented to him.
whyNot.1: Excluding Jordan breaches the person-centred approach NG43 requires.
whyNot.3: NG43 includes independent living and housing in transition planning.

reteach.title: A bridge, not a cliff
reteach.question: What turns the 'cliff edge' at 18 into a bridge?

blocks.body: Start early (year 9). One named worker who stays for at least 6 months either side. The young person at the centre, with goals agreed with them. Adult services met before transfer, at a stable time, with the same practitioner for the first two appointments.

blocks.text: Turning 18 changes who makes decisions (the young person, with support), not whether support continues.

explain.body: NG43 1.2.1: from year 9 (age 13 or 14) at the latest; immediately if entering services close to transfer; from 15 and a half for young people leaving care.

test.q: A young person with a learning disability is referred to children's services at 17. When should transition planning start?
options: Immediately
At age 18
In year 9
After a year
test.why: NG43 1.2.1: for young people entering the service close to the point of transfer, planning should start immediately.

whyNot.1: Waiting until 18 leaves no time to plan.
whyNot.3: A year's delay would pass the point of transfer.

explain.body: One practitioner with a meaningful relationship coordinates transition, links professionals, supports the family and stays a minimum of 6 months before and after transfer.

test.q: Who can act as a young person's named worker under NICE NG43?
options: A senior manager from the adult services team
Any practitioner the parents choose for the role
Someone they have a meaningful relationship with
The consultant paediatrician leading their care
test.why: NG43 1.2.6: the named worker could be a nurse, youth worker, AHP, GP or existing keyworker, and should be someone with whom the young person has a meaningful relationship.

whyNot.0: Senior managers are accountable for strategy, not named workers.
whyNot.1: The young person helps identify the named worker (1.2.5).
whyNot.3: Many practitioners can take the role; it is not fixed to the lead consultant.

explain.body: Care Act s58 child's needs assessment before 18 if likely adult needs. EHC plan can run to the end of the academic year at 25 (CFA 2014 s46). MCA from 16.

test.q: From what age does the Mental Capacity Act 2005 generally apply?
test.why: The MCA 2005 generally applies to people aged 16 and over.

whyNot.0: 14 is the age annual health checks start, not the MCA age.

explain.body: Adult practitioners meet the young person before transfer; same practitioner for the first 2 attended appointments; if they disengage, contact and follow up rather than discharge.

test.q: What does NICE NG43 recommend for the first appointments in adult health services after transfer?
options: A different clinician each time for variety
Group sessions with other young adults
The same practitioner for the first two
Telephone contact for the whole first year
test.why: NG43 1.4.4: ensure the young person sees the same healthcare practitioner for the first 2 attended appointments after transfer.

whyNot.0: Continuity, not variety, is the aim.
whyNot.1: Group sessions are not what NG43 specifies.
whyNot.3: NG43 does not limit contact to telephone.
